title: Cohort retention analysis
objective: Group customers into cohorts by when they started, measure how many come back in each later period, and present it as retention counts, rates and a cohort matrix.
context: The growth team wants to know whether customers acquired in 2025 stick around as well as the 2024 ones. Averages across all customers hide this; cohorts compare like with like — customers at the same age, regardless of calendar date.

exercises.title: Assign each customer a cohort month
exercises.question: Growth needs every customer tagged with their acquisition month.
exercises.prompt: Use valid orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')) of known customers (INNER JOIN customers — the orphan order 31 is excluded). Return customer_id, first_order_date (their earliest valid order date) and cohort_month ('YYYY-MM' of first_order_date). One row per customer.
hints: The cohort is defined by each customer's FIRST valid order.
GROUP BY customer_id with MIN(order_date).
SELECT o.customer_id, MIN(o.order_date) AS first_order_date, strftime('%Y-%m', MIN(o.order_date)) AS cohort_month FROM orders o JOIN customers c ... WHERE ... GROUP BY o.customer_id;
exercises.why: Every cohort analysis starts with a stable, one-row-per-customer cohort assignment. Getting the 'what counts as an order' filter right here propagates everywhere.

recall.q: Why exclude cancelled orders when finding the first order?
recall.a: A cancelled order isn't a real purchase; counting it would put customers (e.g. #16) in a cohort they never truly joined.

exercises.snowflake: DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(o.order_date)) AS cohort_month (a DATE, not text).

exercises.title: Cohort sizes by quarter
exercises.question: How many new customers did we acquire each quarter?
exercises.prompt: Same customer/order definition as 38.1 (valid orders of known customers). Assign each customer the quarter of their first valid order as cohort_quarter (format 'YYYY-Qn', e.g. '2024-Q1'). Return cohort_quarter and new_customers (number of customers in that cohort). Order by cohort_quarter.
hints: Two levels of aggregation: first per customer (MIN), then per quarter (COUNT).
Quarter label: strftime('%Y', d) || '-Q' || ((CAST(strftime('%m', d) AS INTEGER) + 2) / 3).
WITH first_order AS (... MIN(order_date) ... GROUP BY customer_id) SELECT <quarter label> AS cohort_quarter, COUNT(*) AS new_customers FROM first_order GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY cohort_quarter;
exercises.why: Cohort size is the denominator of every retention rate — and a growth KPI by itself (new customers per period).

recall.q: What is the denominator of a cohort retention rate?
recall.a: The cohort size: the number of customers whose first activity fell in that cohort period.

exercises.snowflake: DATE_TRUNC('quarter', first_date) AS cohort_quarter, COUNT(*) ... GROUP BY 1

exercises.title: Months since first order
exercises.question: For each customer, list the months they were active and how many months after their first order each was.
exercises.prompt: Valid orders of known customers (as in 38.1). Return one row per customer per active month: customer_id, cohort_month ('YYYY-MM' of their first valid order), order_month ('YYYY-MM' of a month with at least one valid order) and months_since_first (calendar-month difference: (year*12 + month) of order_month minus the same for cohort_month; 0 for the first month).
hints: Join each order back to the customer's first order date.
Month index = year*12 + month; the difference of two indexes is the calendar-month gap. Use DISTINCT so two orders in one month give one row.

SELECT DISTINCT a.customer_id, strftime('%Y-%m', f.first_date), strftime('%Y-%m', a.order_date), (CAST(strftime('%Y',a.order_date) AS INTEGER)*12 + CAST(strftime('%m',a.order_date) AS INTEGER)) - (same for f.first_date) FROM activity a JOIN first_order f ...
exercises.why: The period index aligns customers by age, not calendar — month 3 means 'three months after joining' for everyone.

recall.q: Why not use (julianday(b) - julianday(a)) / 30 for months since first order?
recall.a: Day counts don't map cleanly onto calendar months; cohort tables count calendar-month boundaries (Jan 31 → Feb 1 is month 1).

exercises.snowflake: DATEDIFF('month', first_date, order_date) AS months_since_first — it counts month boundaries, exactly this index.

exercises.title: Quarterly retention counts
exercises.question: How many customers of each quarterly cohort were active 0, 1, 2… quarters after their first order?
exercises.prompt: Valid orders of known customers (as in 38.1). Quarter index of a date = year*4 + (month-1)/3 (integer division). Return cohort_quarter ('YYYY-Qn' of the first valid order), quarters_since_first (quarter index of an order minus quarter index of the first order) and active_customers (distinct customers with at least one valid order in that quarter). Order by cohort_quarter, quarters_since_first.
hints: Compute a quarter index once in the activity CTE; MIN of it per customer is the cohort's index.
COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) — a customer with two orders in one quarter counts once.
GROUP BY cohort_quarter, (q_idx - first_q_idx) and COUNT(DISTINCT a.customer_id).
exercises.why: This long table (cohort, period, count) is the canonical retention dataset — every chart and matrix is built from it.

recall.q: Why COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) rather than COUNT(*) in retention counts?
recall.a: Retention counts customers, not orders: a customer with three orders in a period is one retained customer.

exercises.snowflake: DATEDIFF('quarter', DATE_TRUNC('quarter', first_date), DATE_TRUNC('quarter', order_date)) AS quarters_since_first

exercises.title: Quarterly retention rates
exercises.question: Turn the counts into rates so cohorts of different sizes can be compared.
exercises.prompt: Extend 38.4: return cohort_quarter, quarters_since_first, cohort_size (customers in the cohort), active_customers and retention_pct (100.0 * active_customers / cohort_size, 0–100 scale, rounded to 1 decimal). Same definitions as 38.4. Order by cohort_quarter, quarters_since_first.
hints: Cohort size = active_customers at quarters_since_first = 0, or COUNT(*) of first_order per cohort.
Build counts and sizes as separate CTEs and join them on cohort_quarter.

... SELECT c.cohort_quarter, c.quarters_since_first, s.cohort_size, c.active_customers, ROUND(100.0 * c.active_customers / s.cohort_size, 1) AS retention_pct FROM counts c JOIN sizes s USING (cohort_quarter) ORDER BY ...
exercises.why: Rates make a 4-customer cohort comparable to a 2-customer cohort. (With cohorts this small, one customer swings the rate by 25–50 points — always show cohort_size next to the rate.)

recall.q: What is retention_pct at quarters_since_first = 0, by construction?
recall.a: 100% — every customer is active in their own first quarter.

exercises.snowflake: Alternative for cohort_size: FIRST_VALUE(active_customers) OVER (PARTITION BY cohort_quarter ORDER BY quarters_since_first).

exercises.title: Retention matrix with censoring
exercises.question: The board deck wants the classic triangle: one row per cohort, columns for quarters 1–4 after acquisition.
exercises.prompt: Same definitions as 38.5 (valid orders of known customers; quarter index = year*4 + (month-1)/3). Return cohort_quarter, cohort_size, and q1_pct, q2_pct, q3_pct, q4_pct = percentage (0–100, rounded to 1 decimal) of the cohort active exactly 1, 2, 3, 4 quarters after their first quarter. Use 0 when that quarter is observable but nobody was active, and NULL when that quarter lies after 2025-Q4 (the as-of date is 2025-12-31). Order by cohort_quarter.
hints: Pivot the (cohort, k) counts with COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN k = 1 THEN customer_id END) etc.
As-of quarter index = 2025*4 + 3 (2025-Q4). A cell is observable if first_q_idx + k <= that; otherwise CASE ... END yields NULL.

per_cohort CTE: cohort_quarter, MIN(first_q_idx), COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS cohort_size, a1..a4; final SELECT: CASE WHEN first_q_idx + 1 <= 2025*4+3 THEN ROUND(100.0*a1/cohort_size,1) END AS q1_pct, ...
exercises.why: Distinguishing 'nobody came back' (0) from 'too early to know' (NULL) is what makes a retention triangle honest. Never use date('now') — fix the as-of date so results are reproducible.

recall.q: Why show NULL rather than 0 for future cells of a young cohort?
recall.a: Because those periods haven't happened yet as of the as-of date; 0 would falsely claim everyone churned.

exercises.snowflake: Pre-aggregate retention_pct per (cohort, k), then PIVOT (MAX(retention_pct) FOR k IN (1,2,3,4)); censoring: IFF(DATEADD('quarter', k, cohort_quarter) <= '2025-10-01', pct, NULL).

exercises.title: Signup cohorts: converted within 90 days
exercises.question: Marketing measures acquisition by signup date. Of each quarter's signups, how many placed a valid order within 90 days?
exercises.prompt: Cohort = quarter of customers.signup_date (signup_quarter, 'YYYY-Qn'); include ALL customers, even those who never ordered. A customer converted if their first valid order (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')) is on or before signup_date + 90 days (julianday(first_order) - julianday(signup_date) <= 90). Return signup_quarter, signups, converted_90d and conversion_pct (100.0 * converted_90d / signups, rounded to 1 decimal). Order by signup_quarter.
hints: Start FROM customers and LEFT JOIN each customer's first valid order — non-buyers must stay in the denominator.
For non-buyers first_date is NULL, so the <= 90 comparison is NULL and the CASE falls to ELSE 0.

SELECT <signup quarter label>, COUNT(*) AS signups, SUM(CASE WHEN julianday(f.first_date) - julianday(c.signup_date) <= 90 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS converted_90d, ... FROM customers c LEFT JOIN first_order f ... GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY signup_quarter;
exercises.why: Signup cohorts answer 'is our onboarding converting?', while first-order cohorts answer 'do buyers come back?'. The LEFT JOIN is what keeps never-buyers (18, 19, 20) in the denominator.

recall.q: Why must this query start from customers with a LEFT JOIN?
recall.a: So customers who never ordered still count as signups; an inner join would inflate the conversion rate.

exercises.snowflake: COUNT_IF(f.first_date <= DATEADD('day', 90, c.signup_date)) AS converted_90d, grouped by DATE_TRUNC('quarter', c.signup_date).

worked_example.question: When did each customer place their first valid order?
worked_example.sql:
SELECT o.customer_id,
       MIN(o.order_date) AS first_order_date,
       strftime('%Y', MIN(o.order_date)) || '-Q'
         || ((CAST(strftime('%m', MIN(o.order_date)) AS INTEGER) + 2) / 3) AS cohort_quarter
FROM orders AS o
JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
GROUP BY o.customer_id
ORDER BY first_order_date
LIMIT 6;
worked_example.explanation: MIN(order_date) per customer is the cohort anchor. The INNER JOIN to customers drops the orphan order 31 (customer 99), and the status filter means customer 16 (only a cancelled order) is not a customer for this analysis at all.

recipe:
**Recipe: cohort retention in 5 moves**

1. **Activity table:** one row per customer per active period (here: valid orders of known customers,
   `order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')` joined to `customers`).
2. **Cohort:** each customer's first period — `MIN(order_date)` per customer (or `signup_date`).
3. **Period index:** periods since the cohort start. Month index trick in SQLite:
   `year*12 + month`; quarter index: `year*4 + (month-1)/3`. Subtract the cohort's index.
4. **Count:** `COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)` per (cohort, period_index).
5. **Rate:** divide by the cohort size (period 0 = 100%), optionally pivot periods into columns.

```sql
WITH activity AS (...),                          -- customer_id, order_date
first_order AS (SELECT customer_id, MIN(order_date) AS first_date FROM activity GROUP BY customer_id),
idx AS (SELECT a.customer_id,
               strftime('%Y-%m', f.first_date) AS cohort_month,
               (CAST(strftime('%Y', a.order_date) AS INT)*12 + CAST(strftime('%m', a.order_date) AS INT))
             - (CAST(strftime('%Y', f.first_date) AS INT)*12 + CAST(strftime('%m', f.first_date) AS INT))
                 AS months_since_first
        FROM activity a JOIN first_order f USING (customer_id))
SELECT cohort_month, months_since_first, COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS active_customers
FROM idx GROUP BY 1, 2;
```

**Right-censoring:** a cohort from 2025-Q4 *cannot* have "4 quarters later" data as of 2025-12-31.
Show those cells as NULL, not 0 — zero would look like everyone churned.
With only ~16 customers, quarterly cohorts are far more readable than monthly ones.
snowflake_notes:
Snowflake makes the date math much shorter:

```sql
WITH activity AS (
    SELECT o.customer_id, o.order_date
    FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
),
cohorts AS (
    SELECT customer_id,
           order_date,
           DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id)) AS cohort_month
    FROM activity
)
SELECT cohort_month,
       DATEDIFF('month', cohort_month, DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)) AS months_since_first,
       COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS active_customers
FROM cohorts
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2;
```

- `DATEDIFF('month', a, b)` counts month *boundaries* crossed (Jan 31 → Feb 1 = 1), which is exactly the
  calendar-month index cohort tables want. Same for `DATEDIFF('quarter', ...)`.
- Pivot the retention matrix with `PIVOT (COUNT(DISTINCT ...) ...)`? Not allowed — PIVOT takes a simple aggregate
  over a column; pre-aggregate, then `PIVOT (MAX(retention_pct) FOR months_since_first IN (0,1,2,3))`.
- `DATEADD('day', 90, signup_date)` for "within 90 days" windows.
common_mistakes: Counting orders instead of distinct customers in retention cells.
Defining the cohort from all orders (including cancelled) instead of valid ones.
Showing 0 for periods that haven't happened yet (right-censoring) instead of NULL.
Using day differences / 30 for month indexes instead of calendar-month arithmetic.
Using date('now') as the as-of date — results change every day; fix it ('2025-12-31').
Inner-joining signups to orders, which drops never-buyers from the denominator.
recall: Name the three columns of a long-format retention table.
cohort (start period), period index (periods since start), active customer count (or rate).
How do you compute a calendar-month index difference in SQLite? In Snowflake?
SQLite: (y2*12 + m2) - (y1*12 + m1) from strftime parts. Snowflake: DATEDIFF('month', d1, d2).
What's right-censoring in a cohort table?
Later periods of young cohorts aren't observable yet as of the as-of date; they must be NULL/blank, not 0.
